text: Today we're launching cve.now , a free feed of CVEs and security advisories for agents and the teams that use them. cve.now merges siloed data sources (the CVE List , CISA's list of exploited vulnerabilities , EPSS , and OSV ) into a single unified feed of vulnerabilities that can be conveniently searched, filtered, and consumed by agents. It provides a plain-English explanation of each vulnerability and makes it easy to identify which ones you're impacted by. The feed is available as RSS, JSON, or API, and there's an MCP server that gives your coding agent direct access to this critical information. Best of all, it's free. cve.now requires no login, signup, or API key. You can get started immediately. October 21st was a rough day for anyone running software in production. First, we learned about PHP2Shell : two bugs in core PHP that make it possible for attackers to run commands on your server with a single POST request. Amazon reported an exploit attempt four days prior to disclosure, which means attackers have a head start. Then there was the LiteLLM supply chain attack . Attackers managed to publish a malicious version of LiteLLM to both PyPI and Docker, where it was downloaded by thousands of users. This version, 1.107.0, steals cloud and AI credentials from anyone unfortunate enough to run it. There was also a Node.js security update (versions 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4), which addressed 10 security vulnerabilities. One of these stands out as particularly severe: a Brotli decoder bug that allows for remote code execution. Finally, the Railway hack. A Railway disclosure published on Wednesday, October 21 reported unauthorized access to Railway's internal systems, including customer environment variables, API keys, and DB credentials. Much of the industry spent the next 24 hours rotating keys. If this is the new normal, how are software teams expected to keep up? The answer might seem obvious. Many of these issues show up first as a CVE or security advisory. If you subscribe to the sources that publish this information, you can find out fast and have your agent check whether you're affected, pushing patches when necessary. Unfortunately, this isn't as simple as it sounds. CVE data sources have major problems that make it hard for software teams to use them effectively. There are three main ones today. First, data is fragmented. If you don't have all four, it's hard to evaluate risk and make prioritization decisions. Second, there's no “trigger.” In general, agents only act when you ask them to, which means a critical CVE can sit for hours before a team member notices and directs their agent to investigate. Running your agent on a loop helps, but this approach is costly, and you still lose time between intervals. Third, the sheer number of vulnerabilities is overwhelming. More than 48,000 CVEs were published last year - over 130 a day. In 2026, the number is certain to be much higher. Most of these CVEs don't apply to you, but without effective filters, it's hard to identify the ones that do. cve.now is a free feed of CVEs and security advisories that addresses these problems. Most importantly, cve.now is free for anyone to use. No login, signup, or API key required. Every 5 minutes, cve.now pulls new and updated records from the CVE List, CISA KEV, EPSS, and OSV. It merges these into one entry per CVE by cross-checking identifiers - never by fuzzy-matching. This means a CVE and its associated GitHub advisory will never show up twice, and two different bugs will never collapse into a single entry. Merging is valuable not just for convenience, but also for determining which vulnerabilities actually matter. Take CVE-2025-61624 , a Fortinet bug from last week. Its severity score is 5.4, a “medium” - but CISA says attackers are actively exploiting it. An agent looking only at the CVE record would tell you to ignore it. On cve.now, it appears in the critical feed , making it hard to miss. The critical feed is deterministic, not AI-driven. cve.now considers an entry to be “critical” if any of the following are true: It's important that the critical feed is deterministic, not AI-driven, because error and inaccuracy are unacceptable in this context. It also helps with cost: by subscribing to the critical feed, you can avoid paying an agent to triage tens or hundreds of CVEs every day. After merging the data, cve.now uses AI to write a short, plain-English summary of each entry. The summary is labeled as AI-written, and the original description is always included right below it. Facts like severity, exploitation status, and affected versions always come from the source data, never the model. Everything is served as RSS , Atom , and JSON feeds, filterable by technology or package ecosystem (e.g., just PHP, or just npm). There's also a JSON API and an MCP server. cve.now is easy to use. You can add the MCP server to your coding agent by pasting this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any other agent that supports MCP: Add the cve.now MCP server to your MCP configuration: name "cve-now", remote Streamable HTTP server at https://cve.now/mcp, no authentication. Then confirm the tools get_vulnerability, list_feed and check_stack are available, and run check_stack on this project's lockfile to list any known vulnerabilities in my dependencies. Afterwards, your agent can look up any CVE and check your dependencies against recent vulnerabilities on its own. If you use Slack, you can install Slack's RSS app , then subscribe to a channel: /feed subscribe https://cve.now/feed?filter=critical New critical CVEs will show up in your Slack channel as they appear. cve.now is powerful but not without limitations. Here are the key ones today: Last, and this one is very important: cve.now does not include information or entries for incidents that never received a CVE. Many security incidents, including the recent Railway hack, do not qualify as CVEs and will never receive this assignment. These incidents will not show up in cve.now today - or in any vulnerability feed, for that matter. We may consider incorporating them in the future, but for now, you should not treat cve.now as your exclusive source of security notices. Security is top of mind for everyone right now, including Sazabi . Whenever a major security incident occurs, our customers ask the same question: “Are we affected?” Sazabi aims to help them answer this question as quickly as possible. Just as important are the vulnerabilities that our customers may not be aware of. Again, Sazabi has a responsibility to notify our customers about these and help them implement mitigations as quickly as possible. cve.now is how we deliver on this promise. By consuming signals from cve.now, Sazabi is able to automatically check if customers are affected by new security vulnerabilities in real time and notify them immediately. The cve.now feed and MCP server are enabled by default for every Sazabi customer and project. We recognized that this data source would be useful to everyone, not just Sazabi customers, so we made it free and publicly available.
